content: 1. Acquisition: This refers to the process of measuring and storing image data during an MRI scan. 2. Apex of the Heart: The apex is the blunt, rounded tip of the heart, which is formed by the left ventricle. The myocardial tissue in this region is thinner compared to other parts of the ventricle. 3. Artifact: An artifact is a false structure or feature in an image or data that is caused by the imaging technique or equipment, rather than the actual object being imaged. 4. Axial: This describes a plane or section created by cutting the body or a part of it at right angles to its long axis. When the body is upright, this cut is parallel to the horizon. 5. B₀: This is the conventional symbol for the constant magnetic field generated by the large magnet in an MRI scanner. 6. B₁: This is the conventional symbol used to denote the radiofrequency (RF) magnetic field in MRI. 7. Base of the Heart: The base of the heart is the region formed by the atria and the roots of the great vessels, located opposite the apex. It is considered the top of the heart. 8. Cine: This refers to a series of rapidly recorded sequential images displayed as a dynamic movie. It is often used to study the motion of joints or parts of the spine. 9. Contrast: Contrast in MRI refers to the relative difference in signal intensities between two adjacent regions of an image. It is influenced by parameters such as proton density, T1, and T2 relaxation times. 10. Coronal: This describes a plane or section made by cutting across the body from side to side, parallel to the coronal suture of the skull. 11. Echo Planar Imaging (EPI): This is a technique that uses rapid gradient reversal pulses to generate a series of gradient echo signals, reducing signal loss or dephasing. 12. Echo Train: This is a series of 180° RF rephasing pulses and their corresponding echoes used in a Fast Spin Echo (FSE) pulse sequence. 13. Fast Spin Echo (FSE): This is a pulse sequence characterized by a series of rapidly applied 180° rephasing pulses and multiple echoes, with phase encoding gradients altered for each echo. 14. Fat Saturation (Fat-Sat): This is a specialized technique that selectively saturates fat protons before acquiring data, minimizing their signal. It requires a highly homogeneous magnetic field and precise frequency calibration. 15. Fat Suppression: This process removes the effects of fat from MRI images, often using Short TI Inversion Recovery (STIR) sequences. 16. Field of View (FOV): This is the size of the spatial encoding area of the image, typically measured in square centimeters (cm²). 17. Field Echo (FE): Also known as Gradient Echo, this is an echo produced by reversing the direction of the magnetic field gradient to cancel out position-dependent phase shifts. 18. Flip Angle (FA): This is the angle to which the net magnetization is rotated relative to the main magnetic field direction by an RF excitation pulse. It defines the excitation angle for a Field Echo pulse sequence. 19. Fourier Transform (FT): This is a mathematical process used in MRI to analyze and separate the amplitude and phase of individual frequency components in the signal, allowing spatial information to be reconstructed from raw data. 20. Gadolinium (Gd): Gadolinium is a non-toxic paramagnetic contrast agent used in MRI. When injected, it shortens T1 relaxation times in its surroundings, enhancing signal intensities. 21. Image Acquisition Time: This is the time required to collect a complete set of image data. It includes the additional time needed for image reconstruction. 22. Image Reconstruction: This is the mathematical process of converting raw signals obtained during data acquisition into a visual image. 23. Inversion Recovery: This is an imaging sequence involving successive 180° and 90° pulses, producing a heavily T1-weighted signal. It is defined by parameters such as inversion time (TI), repetition time (TR), and echo time (TE). 24. Inversion Time (TI): This is the time interval between the 180° inversion pulse and the 90° excitation pulse in an Inversion Recovery sequence. 25. K-Space: This is a data acquisition matrix containing raw image data before image processing. In 2D Fourier Transform (2DFT), each line corresponds to the digitized NMR signal at a specific phase-encoding level. 26. Larmor Equation: This equation states that the precession frequency of a nuclear magnetic moment is directly proportional to the product of the magnetic field strength (B₀) and the gyromagnetic ratio (γ). Mathematically, ω = γB₀. 27. Larmor Frequency: This is the frequency at which magnetic resonance in a nucleus can be excited and detected. It varies directly with the magnetic field strength and is typically in the radiofrequency range. 28. Magnetic Resonance: This is the absorption or emission of energy by atomic nuclei in an external magnetic field after the application of RF excitation pulses at frequencies satisfying the Larmor equation. 29. Magnetic Resonance Angiography (MRA): This is an MRI technique used to visualize specific vascular structures, such as the Circle of Willis or carotid arteries. 30. Maximum Intensity Projection (MIP): This is a processing method for MRA images that records the maximum intensity along a ray passing through an angiographic volume. 31. MRI Imaging: This involves using magnetic resonance principles to produce diagnostic images of the human body, based on tissue parameters such as proton density, T1 relaxation time, T2 relaxation time, and flow characteristics. 32. Noise: This refers to unwanted background interference or disturbances that degrade image quality. 33. Oblique: This describes a plane or section that is not perpendicular to the XYZ coordinate system, such as the long and short axis views of the heart. 34. Orthogonal: This refers to a plane or section that is perpendicular to the XYZ coordinate system. 35. Phase Contrast: This is an MRA technique that uses changes in the phase shifts of flowing protons in the region of interest to create an image. 36. Phase Encoding: This is the process of spatially locating an MR signal by altering the phase of spins in one dimension using a pulsed magnetic field gradient. 37. Pixel: This is the smallest discrete two-dimensional element of a digital image display. 38. Planar Imaging: This involves the slow gyration of the axis of a spinning body, tracing out a cone due to the application of a torque. 39. Pulse Sequence: This is a predefined set of RF and gradient pulses, repeated multiple times during a scan, which controls NMR signal reception and affects the characteristics of the resulting MRI images. 40. Receiver: This is the part of the MRI equipment that detects and amplifies RF signals picked up by the receiver coil. It includes a preamplifier, NMR signal amplifier, and demodulator. 41. Receiver Coil: This is a coil or antenna placed within the imaging volume and connected to the receiver circuitry to detect the NMR signal. Some coils can be used for both transmission and reception. 42. Reconstruction: This is the mathematical process of producing a displayed image from raw k-space data, typically using Fourier transformation and selective filtering. 43. Region of Interest (ROI): This is the specific area of anatomy being scanned that is of particular importance in the image. 44. Relaxation Time: After excitation, spins return to their equilibrium distribution, with no transverse magnetization and maximum longitudinal magnetization aligned with the static magnetic field. Transverse magnetization decays with a time constant T2, while longitudinal magnetization returns to equilibrium with a time constant T1. 45. Repetition Time (TR): This is the time interval between successive pulse sequences applied to the same slice. It affects image contrast and total scan time. 46. Resonance: This is a large amplitude vibration in a system caused by a small periodic stimulus at or near the system's natural frequency. 47. Sagittal: This describes a plane or section of the body cut from front to back through the sagittal suture of the skull, dividing the body into two parts. 48. Saturation Recovery: This is a pulse sequence that generates a predominantly proton density-dependent signal using a 90° RF excitation pulse and a long repetition time. 49. Selective Excitation: This involves controlling the frequency spectrum of an RF excitation pulse while applying a gradient magnetic field so that only a desired region is excited. 50. Scan Time: This is the total time required to acquire all the data needed to produce the programmed image. 51. Signal Averaging: This is a method to improve the signal-to-noise ratio by averaging several free induction decays (FIDs) obtained under similar conditions. 52. Signal-to-Noise Ratio (SNR): This is the ratio of the amplitude of the received signal to background noise. SNR can be improved by increasing the number of excitations, field of view, or slice thickness. 53. Slice: This refers to the planar region or image slice selection region in MRI. 54. Slice Thickness: This is the thickness of an imaging slice, determined by the distance between points at half the sensitivity of the maximum. 55. Spatial Resolution: This is the ability to distinguish minute adjacent objects or points in an image, typically measured in line pairs per millimeter (lp/mm). 56. Spin Echo (SE): This is the reappearance of the NMR signal after the free induction decay (FID) has apparently decayed, achieved by rephasing dephased spins using specific RF pulse sequences. 57. Steady-State Free Precession: This refers to a field echo or gradient echo sequence where a non-zero steady state develops for both transverse and longitudinal magnetization components. 58. STIR: This stands for Short TI Inversion Recovery, a technique used to suppress fat in MRI images. 59. Surface Coil: This is a type of receiver coil placed directly on or over the region of interest to increase magnetic sensitivity and improve the signal-to-noise ratio. 60. T1: This is the spin-lattice or longitudinal relaxation time, representing the time constant for spins to realign with the external magnetic field after excitation. 61. T1-Weighted: This is an image created using short TE and TR times, where contrast and brightness are predominantly determined by T1 signals. 62. T2: This is the spin-spin or transverse relaxation time, representing the time constant for the loss of phase coherence among spins due to spin-spin interactions. 63. T2: This is the time constant for the loss of phase coherence among spins due to a combination of magnetic field inhomogeneities and spin-spin relaxation. 64. T2-Weighted: This is an image created using longer TE and TR times, where contrast and brightness are predominantly determined by T2 signals. 65. TE (Echo Time): This is the time in milliseconds between the application of the 90° pulse and the peak of the echo signal in Spin Echo and Inversion Recovery sequences. 66. Tesla (T): This is the preferred unit of magnetic flux density, where one Tesla equals 10,000 Gauss. 67. Time of Flight (TOF): This is an MRA technique that relies on the flow of unsaturated blood into a magnetized presaturated slice, creating a bright vascular image without the use of contrast agents. 68. TR (Repetition Time): This is the time interval between successive pulse sequences applied to the same slice, affecting image contrast and total scan time.
